newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- JULY 15.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- JULY 15.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--The surge in the dollar yesterday has put the government on alert to possible inflationary pressures. That issue will be included on the agenda of a meeting between Prime Minister Costas Simitis, National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou and Bank of Greece Governor Lucas Papademos today. Also on the agenda are a possible relaxation of criteria for economic and monetary union and an appraisal of and possible readjustment of economic policies.

--Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos went on the offensive yesterday at ruling PASOK's executive bureau meeting, attacking PASOK members for their criticism of the Madrid agreement on Greek-Turkish relations signed last week. "The party's executive must support and strengthen the government's policy and not attempt to implement other policies," Pangalos was reported as saying.

--US presidential emissary on the Cyprus issue Richard Holbrooke yesterday linked the course to resolving the problem of the divided island with the island's entry to the European Union, following his meeting with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides in New York.

--An ongoing strike by pharamacies has raised the risk of certain medicines running out. As of today, those entitled to medicines through their health funds will be obliged to pay cash. Pharmacists however appear determined to stick to their strike, expected to end on Wednesday.
--Greek shipping magnate Yiannis Latsis came 200th on Forbes list of the wealthiest people in the world. Latsis has an annual income of 2.8 billion dollars.

--"It's difficult for a woman, because she has to prove anew every day that she is worthy," says 36-year-old Georgia Kotidou, the president of the Central Macedonian Technical Chamber of Commerce, the first woman in Greece to be elected to such a position.

--Prime Minister Costas Simitis continues to maintain his personal popularity - although Left Coalition Nikos Constantopoulos beats him out 66.6 percent to 48.9 - despite a lacklustre image for his government, with a majority of those polled in a recent survey saying they are not at all satisfied with the government or the opposition party New Democracy.

--There's reports of tension within ruling party PASOK over top management positions in state-run organisations and enterprises (DEKOs), with Simitis reportedly concerned that the government's plans to introduce private-sector managers going down the drain.
--Changes to building regulations to conserve energy may give land owners the right to add an extra floor to buildings under construction.

--Turkish Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz has sent a letter to his Greek counterpart calling on Athens' help for Turkey to achieve "its European orientation" and to lift the veto on EU funds. Simitis said the support would be forthcoming if Ankara met Greece's preconditions.
--Would-be Archbishops of Greece are jostling for position in case ailing incumbent Serapheim succumbs. Claims of financial mismanagement have taken centre-stage in the battle for the succession.
--Lorries will be restricted from using national roads as of September 15 this year in an effort to bring down the number of road deaths. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
